---
title: "2. Six-Sided Die"
subtitle: "Discrete, flat, and perfectly symmetric"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/clt_helpers.R")
roll_die <- function(k) sample(1:6, size = k, replace = TRUE)
```

## What population am I sampling from?

A fair die: values 1 through 6, each with probability 1/6, simulated with `sample(1:6, replace = TRUE)`. It's **discrete** (only 6 possible values), **bounded**, and **perfectly symmetric**, but it's flat instead of bell-shaped, so its tails are *lighter* than a normal's.

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig-height: 4
plot_population(roll_die, "Population: Fair Six-Sided Die", discrete = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: theory
values <- 1:6
p      <- rep(1/6, 6)
mu     <- sum(values * p)                         # 3.5
sigma  <- sqrt(sum((values - mu)^2 * p))          # sqrt(35/12)
g1     <- sum(((values - mu) / sigma)^3 * p)      # skewness
g2     <- sum(((values - mu) / sigma)^4 * p) - 3  # excess kurtosis
data.frame(mean = mu, sd = sigma, skewness = g1, excess_kurtosis = g2)
```

## What did I expect?

Since the die is symmetric, skewness is 0 at every $n$, so skewness won't be the problem. The issue is the flat shape: excess kurtosis starts at `r round(g2, 3)` (light tails) and shrinks like $g_2/n$. I also expect discreteness to matter at small $n$ because the mean of $n$ rolls can only take $5n + 1$ different values.

```{r}
predicted_n(g1, g2)
```

The theory predicts my kurtosis cutoff is crossed around $n = 3$. I think the Q-Q plot will look "stair-steppy" for a while longer than that because of the discreteness, so my actual guess is somewhere between 3 and 10.

## Which sample sizes did I investigate?

The standard grid from 1 to 500 (same for every population), with $B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")`$ repetitions at each $n$.

## Simulation

```{r}
#| label: simulate
sweep  <- run_sweep(function(n) simulate_means(roll_die, n, B), mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
tab    <- sweep$table
n_star <- chosen_n(tab)
show_table(tab)
```

```{r}
#| label: pictures
#| fig-height: 12
plot_sampling(sweep, c(1, 2, 5, n_star), mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
```

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot_convergence(tab)
```

## Theory vs. simulation

- **Mean:** every simulated mean is within `r round(max(abs(tab$sim_mean - mu)), 3)` of 3.5.
- **Standard error:** simulated SE / $(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ ranged from `r round(min(tab$se_ratio), 3)` to `r round(max(tab$se_ratio), 3)`. The formula works.
- **Shape:** skewness stays near 0 the whole time (largest |skewness| = `r round(max(abs(tab$skewness)), 3)`), exactly as predicted. Kurtosis starts at `r round(tab$ex_kurt[1], 2)` and climbs toward 0.

## When is it approximately normal?

$$
\boxed{n = `r n_star`}
$$

At $n = `r n_star`$ the skewness is `r round(tab$skewness[tab$n == n_star], 3)`, the excess kurtosis is `r round(tab$ex_kurt[tab$n == n_star], 3)`, and the Q-Q correlation is `r round(tab$qq_cor[tab$n == n_star], 4)`. Kurtosis actually passed my cutoff earlier (around $n = 3$, like theory said). The thing that held it back was the **Q-Q correlation**, because with only a handful of possible values the Q-Q plot is a staircase instead of a line.

## What surprised me?

At just $n = 2$ the histogram is already a triangle, and by $n = 5$ it honestly *looks* bell-shaped to the eye. But the Shapiro-Wilk test rejects normality at `r sum(tab$shapiro_p < 0.05)` of the `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes, including $n = 30$ (p = `r format(tab$shapiro_p[tab$n == 30], digits = 2)`). That's not because the shape is wrong. It's because the mean of $n$ dice can only take a limited set of values, and a test with 5,000 values is sensitive enough to notice the data is *discrete*. That's a good example of "statistically detectable" not being the same as "practically important."

```{r}
#| label: save
save_results("Six-Sided Die", tab, n_star,
             "Symmetric, so only light tails + discreteness slow it down")
```
